relationship: Zion in captivity and restored gladness
rationale: Weeping beside Babylon’s rivers at the remembrance of Zion contrasts with the comfort, joyful mouths and gladness when Zion’s captivity is turned back. The comparison follows the named Zion and captivity setting without making the two poems one occasion.

relationship: Captive songs and the joy of restored Zion
rationale: Captors demand songs of Zion here; the return of Zion’s captivity there fills the people’s mouths and tongues with joy. The speakers and circumstances differ, making the requested captive song and restored expression a concrete contrast.

relationship: The Lord’s song abroad and restored Zion’s voice
rationale: The question about singing the Lord’s song on foreign land contrasts with the joyful mouth and tongue when Zion’s captivity is turned back. This does not supply a named location for Psalm 125 beyond Zion’s stated captivity.

relationship: Refusing to forget Jerusalem or Zion
rationale: The speaker binds himself not to forget Jerusalem; Isaiah answers Zion’s complaint of being forgotten with the Lord’s promise not to forget her and the image of her walls on His hands. Human self-imprecation and divine assurance remain distinct.

relationship: A tongue stuck to the throat
rationale: The conditional curse for failing to remember Jerusalem uses the tongue clinging to the throat, while Psalm 21 describes that condition amid mortal distress. The shared bodily image does not identify the occasions.

relationship: Edom’s participation in Jerusalem’s calamity
rationale: The psalm asks remembrance of Edom’s sons urging Jerusalem’s destruction. Obadiah’s address to Idumea describes opposition when strangers entered Jerusalem and forbids rejoicing, entering and attacking on the day of destruction. The specific quotations and actions are not collapsed into one speech.

relationship: Babylon repaid according to what she did
rationale: The psalm calls happy the one repaying Babylon the repayment she gave; Jeremiah commands that Babylon be repaid according to her works and treated as she treated others. Both explicitly name Babylon and reciprocal recompense.

relationship: Children dashed in judgment against Babylon
rationale: The psalm’s violent blessing concerning Babylon’s infants corresponds to Isaiah’s Babylon oracle describing children dashed before their parents. Isaiah does not specify the psalm’s rock, and the comparison reports the texts rather than extending their command to another setting.

relationship: Wholehearted thanksgiving and music to God
rationale: Both first-person prayers promise thanksgiving with the whole heart and music or sung praise to God. Psalm 137 adds heard speech and angels; Psalm 9 adds the recounting of wonders.

relationship: Bowing toward the holy temple
rationale: Both speakers bow toward God’s holy temple in a context naming His mercy. Psalm 137 adds thanksgiving for mercy and truth; Psalm 5 describes entering the house and bowing in fear.

relationship: Hear quickly on the day of calling
rationale: The petition on whatever day the speaker calls, asking to be heard quickly, closely repeats Psalm 101’s concluding plea. Psalm 137’s strengthening of the soul is an additional element.

relationship: All earth’s kings respond to the Lord
rationale: The summons for all earth’s kings to thank the Lord after hearing His words corresponds to all the kings of the earth fearing His glory in Psalm 101. Thanksgiving and fear are distinguished.

relationship: Singing in view of the Lord’s great glory
rationale: Singing in the Lord’s ways because His glory is great corresponds to announcing His glory and declaring the Lord great and greatly to be praised. The passages unite the stated glory, greatness and sung praise without treating ways and nations as the same object.

relationship: The high Lord attends to the lowly
rationale: The Lord’s height and regard for the lowly parallel His high dwelling and looking upon lowly things, followed by raising the poor. Psalm 137’s knowledge of the lofty from afar is not imported into the target.

relationship: Preservation amid affliction and hostile power
rationale: The speaker’s life is preserved amid affliction and enemies’ anger; Psalm 17 describes enemies overtaking him on the day of affliction and the Lord becoming his support and rescuer. The right-hand wording belongs to Psalm 137, not the selected target.

relationship: A plea concerning the work of God’s hands
rationale: The plea not to neglect the works of God’s hands can be compared with Job’s appeal that those hands made him, followed by his complaint of being struck and remembrance of life and mercy. The speakers’ differing expectations are preserved.

relationship: Divine testing of the speaker
rationale: Psalm 138 begins by affirming that the Lord tested and knew the speaker; Psalm 25 asks the Lord to test and try the speaker’s kidneys and heart. An accomplished testing and a requested testing are distinguished.

relationship: The Lord knows human reasonings
rationale: Knowledge of the speaker’s reasonings from afar corresponds to the Lord knowing human reasonings in Psalm 93. The latter calls them futile, a judgment not stated in this source unit.

relationship: Human ways and tracks before God
rationale: God traces and foresees the speaker’s ways here; Proverbs places a man’s ways before God’s eyes and says He watches all his tracks. The psalm’s measuring cord is not supplied to Proverbs.

relationship: God’s forming hands upon the person
rationale: The Lord’s forming the speaker and placing His hand upon him corresponds to Job’s assertion that God’s hands molded and made him. Job’s subsequent complaint that God changed and struck him gives the comparison a different emotional setting.

relationship: Wonderful divine knowledge beyond the speaker
rationale: The speaker cannot reach God’s wondrous knowledge; Job acknowledges great and wonderful things he did not understand. Neither statement is expanded into knowledge of an unstated event.

relationship: No hiding from God’s presence
rationale: The questions about fleeing God’s Spirit and face correspond to the Lord’s question whether someone hiding can escape His sight and His filling heaven and earth. The different terms Spirit, face and sight remain intact.

relationship: Heaven and Hades cannot remove divine reach
rationale: Both passages explicitly pair ascent to heaven and descent into Hades with God’s presence or reach. The psalm affirms presence; Amos announces inescapable judgment.

relationship: Departure across the sea cannot escape the Lord
rationale: Within the psalm’s question about fleeing God’s face, settling at the sea’s farthest reaches can be compared with Jonah’s attempt to sail to Tarshish from the Lord’s presence and the Lord’s action upon the sea. No geographical identity for the psalm’s destination is asserted.

relationship: Divine handholding and guidance
rationale: Both passages combine God holding the speaker’s hand with divine guidance. Psalm 138 says God’s right hand holds him; Psalm 72 says God grasped the speaker’s right hand and guided him in counsel.

relationship: Darkness does not exclude divine knowledge
rationale: The psalm says darkness is not dark from God and night is lit like day; Daniel says He reveals dark things and knows what is in darkness and light. The comparison preserves Daniel’s actual knowledge wording rather than adding a different concluding light clause.

relationship: Divine support from the mother’s womb
rationale: Both speakers explicitly describe being supported from the womb. Psalm 138 adds the acquiring of kidneys; Psalm 70 names shelter from the mother’s belly.

relationship: The person wonderfully fashioned by God
rationale: Thanksgiving for the speaker’s wonderful making corresponds to Job’s description of God molding him and clothing or threading his body together. The relation is bodily divine workmanship; Job’s distressed protest is not turned into thanksgiving.

relationship: Hidden bodily formation and God’s works
rationale: The psalm says the speaker’s bone and secretly made substance were not hidden from God; Ecclesiastes uses bones in a pregnant woman’s womb to illustrate human ignorance of God’s works. Divine knowledge and human ignorance are contrasted without equating earth’s lowest places with the womb.

relationship: Separation from sinners and men of blood
rationale: The source turns men of blood away while addressing God concerning sinners; Psalm 25 asks not to have the speaker’s life destroyed together with ungodly people and men of bloodshed. The psalmist’s separation is shared, while the source’s conditional opening is preserved.

relationship: The speaker’s aversion to God’s opponents
rationale: The speaker’s hatred of those hating the Lord corresponds to hatred of an assembly of evildoers and refusal to sit with the ungodly. This is a comparison of stated opposition, not an equation of every named group or person.

relationship: Declared hatred of those opposed to God’s law
rationale: Complete hatred of the Lord’s enemies can be compared with the declared hatred of lawbreakers alongside love of His law. The target identifies lawbreakers; it does not repeat the source’s complete-hatred wording.

relationship: Testing the inward person
rationale: Both petitions ask God to test the speaker and examine the heart. Psalm 138 adds knowledge of paths, while Psalm 25 names kidneys and trying by fire.

relationship: Guidance away from a wrong way
rationale: The request to detect a way of lawlessness and guide in an eternal way corresponds to the request for divine guidance in righteousness and a straight way before the speaker. Eternal duration is stated only in Psalm 138.

relationship: Rescue from an unjust man
rationale: The plea to be delivered from an unjust man closely corresponds to Psalm 17’s assurance that the Lord will rescue the speaker from an unjust man. The source also names an evil person.

relationship: Continual hostile thought against the speaker
rationale: The source’s people devise injustices in their heart and array wars all day; Psalm 55 describes all-day hostility toward the speaker’s words and thoughts against him for evil. Literal war is not added to the target.

relationship: Asp venom beneath the lips
rationale: Romans’ written-text sequence includes the poison of asps under their lips, corresponding closely to this psalm’s asp venom beneath their lips. The psalm’s sharpened serpent-like tongue differs from the target’s deceitful tongues.

relationship: Hostile attention to the speaker’s feet
rationale: The plea against unjust people who devise to trip the speaker’s steps corresponds to concealed adversaries watching his heel and waiting for his soul. The relation rests on predatory pursuit expressed through steps or heel.

relationship: A trap concealed on the speaker’s path
rationale: Both passages explicitly place an enemy-hidden trap on the path where the speaker walks. Psalm 139 adds cords, feet and a stumbling block.

relationship: The confession Thou art my God
rationale: Both speakers say to the Lord, Thou art my God, while trusting Him amid surrounding adversaries. Psalm 139 adds a petition to listen; Psalm 30 states the speaker’s hope.

relationship: Do not hand the speaker over to wrongdoers
rationale: Both petitions ask not to be handed over to hostile wrongdoers. Psalm 139’s through-my-desire clause remains uninterpreted; Psalm 26 specifies unjust witnesses and afflicters.

relationship: Trouble returning upon the hostile head
rationale: The trouble of the encirclers’ lips covering them corresponds to trouble returning on an evildoer’s head and injustice descending upon his crown. The source’s compressed head-of-encirclement wording is preserved rather than replaced with a named leader.

relationship: Fire among the punishments of sinners
rationale: The source describes coals falling and being cast into fire; Psalm 10 names fire and sulfur in the sinners’ cup portion after raining traps. The target is not said to rain coals or fire.

relationship: Evil or lawless acts hunt a person
rationale: Evils hunting the unjust man to destruction correspond to lawless acts hunting a man in Proverbs. The target adds bondage by his own sins; the source also judges the talkative man.

relationship: Judgment for poor and needy people
rationale: The Lord’s action for the poor person’s judgment and needy people’s cause corresponds to the royal prayer for judgment of the poor and rescue of the needy. The Lord and the king receiving His judgment are not treated as identical agents.

relationship: Righteousness in God’s presence
rationale: The upright dwelling with God’s presence corresponds to the first-person hope of appearing before His face in righteousness. The thanksgiving clause and satisfaction at appearing glory are distinct additions.

relationship: Crying and pleading to the Lord with the voice
rationale: The source’s cry and plea for attention to the voice of petition closely correspond to the twice-stated voice crying and pleading to the Lord in Psalm 141.

relationship: Prayer and incense offered together
rationale: The comparison of prayer with incense can be read alongside the people praying at the hour when the priest burns incense. The psalm is a prayer-image, whereas Luke narrates simultaneous temple actions.

relationship: Raised hands compared with the evening sacrifice
rationale: The psalm compares the lifting of hands to an evening sacrifice; Exodus prescribes the second daily lamb in the evening as a continual offering. The hands are a comparison, not a claim that the speaker performs the prescribed lamb offering.

relationship: A guard over the mouth against sinful speech
rationale: The request for a guard over the mouth and restraining door around lips corresponds to the speaker placing a guard upon his mouth so as not to sin with his tongue. Petition and stated self-restraint differ.

relationship: Guarding heart and speech from wickedness
rationale: The petition not to turn the heart toward wicked words and sinful excuses corresponds to guarding the heart and removing crooked mouth and unjust lips. Proverbs’ instructions are not represented as the same excuse-making scene.

relationship: Beneficial correction contrasted with an enemy’s pleasant treatment
rationale: The righteous person’s merciful discipline and correction, contrasted with a sinner’s oil, can be compared with open rebuke and trustworthy wounds of a friend against an enemy’s willing kisses. Oil and kisses are distinct images, and the psalm’s final prayer clause is not resolved by the comparison.

relationship: Scattered bones in the speaker’s distress
rationale: The source’s scattered bones beside Hades correspond to the scattered bones in Psalm 21’s bodily distress. The clod-of-earth image and location beside Hades are not added to the target.

relationship: Eyes directed toward the Lord in dependence
rationale: The source directs its eyes toward the Lord and hopes in Him; Psalm 122 lifts eyes to Him and compares that attention with servants awaiting their masters’ hands and divine compassion.

relationship: Protection from sinners’ traps
rationale: The plea to be guarded from the assembled trap and lawless stumbling blocks corresponds to sinners setting a trap while the speaker remains with God’s commandments. The target states fidelity rather than explicitly repeating the source’s protection request.

relationship: Wrongdoers caught in a destructive device
rationale: Sinners falling into his casting net correspond to the evildoer falling into the pit he dug. The source’s his is left unassigned, and a net is not called a pit.

relationship: David and a cave in psalm headings
rationale: Both headings place David in a cave. Psalm 56 explicitly names escape from Saul; Psalm 141 does not name the pursuer or specify which cave. The shared heading information does not prove one historical occasion.

relationship: Repeated voice crying to the Lord
rationale: Both lines repeat with my voice in describing the cry to the Lord. Psalm 141’s second action is pleading; Psalm 76 continues with God attending to the speaker.

relationship: Pouring out the inward plea before God
rationale: The speaker will pour out his plea before God and declare affliction; Psalm 61 tells the assembly to pour out their hearts before Him. The individual plea and the communal heart image are distinguished.

relationship: The failing or despondent spirit within
rationale: The spirit failing within the speaker closely corresponds to the spirit growing despondent within and the troubled heart in Psalm 142. The source continues with God’s knowledge and a trap, details not supplied to the target.

relationship: No human companion or comforter found
rationale: The speaker looks and finds no one recognizing or seeking him; Psalm 68 waits for someone to grieve with him and finds no comforter. Seeking the speaker’s soul is retained as written, not turned into an enemy pursuing him.

relationship: The Lord as the speaker’s portion
rationale: Calling the Lord the speaker’s portion in the land of the living corresponds to the Lord as the portion of inheritance and cup. Neither passage identifies the portion as a literal land allotment.

relationship: Rescue from pursuers stronger than the speaker
rationale: The plea for rescue because pursuers grew stronger than the speaker closely corresponds to Psalm 17’s rescue from powerful enemies who grew stronger than him.

relationship: Release from confinement followed by thanksgiving
rationale: The request to bring the soul out of prison in order to thank God corresponds to rescue, broken bonds and a summons to acknowledge His mercies. The psalm’s soul-prison language is not assigned the target’s particular captivity or cause.

relationship: David endangered by his son
rationale: The heading identifies David pursued by his son; the narrative describes David fleeing the danger from Absalom, identified earlier as his son. It supplies a concrete comparable father-son crisis without proving the poem’s composition date or equating every detail.

relationship: No living person justified before God
rationale: The plea not to enter judgment because no living person will be justified before God corresponds to Romans’ statement that no flesh will be justified before Him by works of law. The law qualification belongs to Romans, not this psalm’s wording.

relationship: Human righteousness before God’s judgment
rationale: Job asks how a mortal can be righteous before the Lord and considers entering judgment with Him; the psalm asks God not to enter judgment with His servant because no living person will be justified before Him. Job’s actual denied-hearing wording is preserved.

relationship: Dwelling in darkness like the long dead
rationale: The enemy’s making the speaker sit in dark places like those long dead closely corresponds to Lamentations’ dwelling in dark places like the dead of ages. The surrounding agents differ and are not equated.

relationship: The spirit loses heart amid distress
rationale: The source’s despondent spirit and troubled heart correspond to Psalm 76’s spirit losing heart after extended speech. Remembering God and gladness in the target are not omitted to claim identical emotional sequences.

relationship: Remembering and meditating on God’s works
rationale: Both speakers remember the Lord’s works and meditate on all His works. Psalm 142 also names ancient days, while Psalm 76 names wonders from the beginning.

relationship: The soul’s longing expressed through waterless land
rationale: The soul like a waterless land for God corresponds to the soul thirsting for Him and flesh longing in a waterless wilderness. The source compares the soul to land; the target situates longing in that landscape.

relationship: Hear lest the speaker resemble those entering the pit
rationale: Psalm 142 asks quick hearing and an unaverted face lest the speaker become like those descending to the pit; Psalm 27 asks that God not remain silent lest he become like those descending into a pit.

relationship: The lifted soul asks to know God’s way
rationale: Both prayers combine lifting the soul to God, trusting or hoping in Him, and asking to know the way to walk. Psalm 142’s morning mercy is an additional specification.

relationship: Refuge in God and rescue from enemies
rationale: The plea for rescue from enemies because the speaker fled to God for refuge corresponds to the confession of God as refuge and rescuer followed by salvation from enemies. No particular flight is inferred.

relationship: God’s good Spirit teaches and guides
rationale: The request to be taught God’s will and led by His good Spirit corresponds to the account of wilderness guidance and the gift of His good Spirit for understanding. Level ground is stated only in the psalm.

relationship: Name and righteousness in divine guidance or restoration
rationale: The source expects life for God’s name’s sake and deliverance in His righteousness; Psalm 22 describes restoration of the soul and guidance in paths of righteousness for His name’s sake. The particular restoration and direction images differ.

relationship: God’s support and destruction of the speaker’s enemies
rationale: The source expects the destruction of enemies and afflicters in God’s mercy; Psalm 53 joins divine support of the soul with turning evils on enemies and a petition to destroy them in truth. Mercy and truth remain the respective grounds stated.

relationship: God trains hands for war
rationale: The blessing of God who trains the speaker’s hands for battle closely repeats the training of hands for war in Psalm 17. The source adds fingers and its Goliath heading; the target adds the bronze bow.

relationship: Goliath’s challenge in the named heading
rationale: The source heading explicitly concerns Goliath; Samuel names Goliath and records his challenge to Israel for single combat. This identifies the named narrative figure without requiring every poetic battle image to be a literal detail of the encounter.

relationship: A cluster of divine refuge and rescue titles
rationale: Both lines call God the speaker’s refuge, helper, rescuer and protector or defender, and express hope in Him. Psalm 143’s subjecting of the people is a further clause, not part of this selected target.

relationship: What is man or a son of man to God
rationale: Both questions pair man and son of man with God’s attention. Psalm 143 asks why God became known to him and takes account of him; Psalm 8 asks why He remembers and visits him.

relationship: Human life passes like a shadow
rationale: The speaker likens a man to futility and his passing days to a shadow; Job describes the mortal’s short life as fleeing like a shadow. Job’s additional flower image is not imported into the psalm.

relationship: Heaven bent down in a smoking divine descent
rationale: The request that the Lord bend heaven and descend, touching mountains so they smoke, corresponds to Psalm 17’s mountain shaking, smoke in divine anger and heaven bent in descent. The source’s touch is not asserted in the target.

relationship: Lightning and arrows scatter adversaries
rationale: Both lines combine divine lightning and arrows with scattering and throwing opponents into confusion. The request and expected action in Psalm 143 correspond to the narrated action of Psalm 17.

relationship: Rescue from many waters from on high
rationale: The plea to send a hand from on high and take the speaker out of many waters closely corresponds to God sending from on high, taking the speaker and removing him from many waters.

relationship: Same-chapter repetition of mouth and right-hand wrongdoing
rationale: This description of foreigners whose mouth spoke futility and whose right hand is a right hand of injustice returns in the later rescue petition. The exact repeated characterization links the petition to the previously described adversaries.

relationship: A new song with a ten-stringed psaltery
rationale: The promise of a new song and music on a ten-stringed psaltery corresponds to the paired commands for that instrument and a new song in Psalm 32.

relationship: Salvation of kings and David the servant
rationale: God’s saving kings and redeeming David His servant corresponds to magnifying His king’s salvations and showing mercy to His anointed, David. Psalm 143’s evil sword is not added to the target.

relationship: Same-chapter return to rescue from the foreigner’s hand
rationale: The later petition repeats rescue from the foreigners’ hand and reproduces their mouth-and-right-hand description from the earlier two verses. This is an internal repeated plea rather than a second historical event.

relationship: Happiness of the people whose God is the Lord
rationale: The closing blessedness of the people whose God is the Lord closely corresponds to the blessed nation whose God is the Lord in Psalm 32. Psalm 143 distinguishes this from what they called happy in the preceding prosperity description.

relationship: Blessing the Lord’s name for ever
rationale: The speaker promises to bless God’s name for the age and age of the age; Psalm 112 blesses the Lord’s name from now and for ever. The royal address of Psalm 144 remains an additional feature.

relationship: Continual blessing and praise
rationale: Blessing God every day and praising His name corresponds to blessing the Lord at every time and praise continually in the mouth. Both explicitly describe the ongoing practice, with different time expressions.

relationship: The Lord great and greatly to be praised
rationale: The same declaration that the Lord is great and greatly to be praised occurs in both passages. Psalm 144 adds limitless greatness, while Psalm 95 adds fearfulness above all gods.

relationship: God’s works and power told to successive generations
rationale: Generation praising God’s works and declaring His power to generation corresponds to announcing mighty acts and wonders so another generation and its children will know. The target gives the intergenerational teaching setting explicitly.

relationship: Declaring divine glory and wonders
rationale: Speech about the magnificence of God’s holy glory and recounting His wonders corresponds to the paired command to announce His glory and wonders among nations and peoples.

relationship: Speaking of fearsome works and divine power
rationale: The declaration of God’s fearsome acts and greatness corresponds to the instruction to say to God how fearsome His works are, through the abundance of His power. The target’s enemies lying is not extended to the source.

relationship: The abundance of divine kindness
rationale: Pouring forth remembrance of abundant kindness corresponds to the exclamation over the great multitude of the Lord’s kindness. Psalm 30 specifies those fearing and hoping in Him; Psalm 144 adds rejoicing in righteousness.

relationship: Compassionate and merciful, abundant in mercy
rationale: The divine attributes compassionate, merciful and abundant in mercy closely parallel the proclamation in Exodus. The psalm says patient, while Exodus says slow to anger and adds true.

relationship: Mercy extending to all God’s works
rationale: The Lord’s kindness to all and compassion over all His works correspond to mercy on all and love for all existing things He made. The comparison follows the expressly universal scope of both passages.

relationship: All God’s works summoned to bless or thank Him
rationale: The summons for all God’s works to thank Him corresponds to all His works being told to bless Him throughout His dominion. Psalm 144 separately calls His holy ones to bless.

relationship: Divine or bestowed kingship, glory and authority
rationale: Speaking of the glory of God’s kingdom and His might can be compared with Daniel’s vision of authority given, glory in worship and an indestructible kingdom. The recipient in Daniel’s vision is not silently equated with the addressee of the psalm.

relationship: Making divine might known to people
rationale: Making God’s might known to the sons of men corresponds to the speaker’s desire to announce His arm and power to the coming generation. Psalm 144 further specifies the glorious kingdom.

relationship: Everlasting dominion and an enduring kingdom
rationale: God’s kingdom of all ages and lordship through every generation correspond to the vision’s everlasting authority and kingdom never destroyed. The comparison concerns their explicit duration while preserving Daniel’s given-authority setting.

relationship: Faithfulness in divine words and works
rationale: The Lord’s faithfulness in His words and holiness in His works correspond to the Lord’s upright word and all His works in faithfulness. The attributes are related but assigned differently in the two sentences.

relationship: The Lord raises the broken down
rationale: The source’s raising all who have been broken down closely repeats the Lord’s raising those broken down in Psalm 145. Psalm 144 additionally names support for the falling.

relationship: Creatures wait for food at the right time
rationale: The eyes of all hoping in God and receiving food at the right time correspond to all waiting for Him to give food at the right time. The target’s creature context is read without limiting the source’s all to a different unstated group.

relationship: The open divine hand fills living things
rationale: The open hand filling every living creature with good pleasure corresponds to God opening His hand and all things being filled with goodness. Good pleasure and goodness are preserved as the respective wording.

relationship: Righteousness and holiness in God’s ways and works
rationale: The Lord’s righteousness in all His ways and holiness in all His works correspond to true works, ways that are judgments, and the declaration that the Lord is righteous and holy.

relationship: The Lord near when people call
rationale: The Lord’s nearness to those calling in truth corresponds to the rhetorical question about the Lord drawing near in all things in which His people call upon Him. The psalm’s truth qualification remains explicit.

relationship: Hearing a plea and rescuing the faithful
rationale: God hearing the plea and saving those who fear Him corresponds to the righteous crying, the Lord hearing and rescuing them. The source also promises fulfillment of their will, which is not supplied to the target.

relationship: The Lord guards those who love Him
rationale: Guarding all who love the Lord corresponds to the address to those loving Him followed by His guarding the souls of His holy ones. The source destroys sinners; the target rescues the guarded people from sinners’ hands.

relationship: Same-chapter closing return to blessing the name for ever
rationale: The final summons to bless God’s holy name for the age and age of the age returns to the opening promise to bless His name with the same duration. The close extends the speaker’s praise to all flesh.

relationship: The soul summoned to praise or bless the Lord
rationale: Praise the Lord, my soul closely parallels Bless the Lord, my soul. The Haggai-and-Zechariah heading is preserved without using this verbal comparison to infer authorship.

relationship: Lifelong praise and music as long as the speaker exists
rationale: Both speakers promise praise or singing throughout life and music to their God as long as they exist. The source’s praise and target’s sing are not treated as identical verbs.

relationship: Do not place trust in humans or rulers
rationale: The warning against trusting rulers and sons of men corresponds to the preference for trust and hope in the Lord over a man or rulers. Psalm 145 expressly grounds the warning in their lack of salvation.

relationship: Departure of spirit and return to earth
rationale: The spirit going out and the person returning to his earth correspond to dust returning to earth and spirit returning to God. Ecclesiastes gives the spirit’s destination; the psalm adds the perishing of reasonings.

relationship: Jacob’s God as helper or supporter
rationale: The happiness of having Jacob’s God as helper corresponds to Jacob’s God being the community’s supporter. The individual hope and communal confession differ.

relationship: Maker of heaven, earth, sea and their contents
rationale: The named creation of heaven, earth, sea and all in them closely corresponds to the same creation list in the Sabbath command. The psalm’s truth kept for ever and Exodus’ six days are distinct additional clauses.

relationship: The Lord does judgment for the wronged
rationale: The Lord doing justice for those wronged corresponds closely to His deeds of mercy and judgment for all who are wronged. The source also feeds the hungry and releases prisoners.

relationship: Release for those held captive
rationale: The Lord’s release of those in fetters corresponds to the commissioned speaker proclaiming release to captives. The Lord as releasing agent and His anointed messenger as proclaimer are distinguished.

relationship: Raising people who have been broken down
rationale: The Lord raising those broken down directly corresponds to Psalm 144’s raising all who have been broken down. The source’s making the blind wise is retained without changing it to the restoration of eyesight.

relationship: God’s care for sojourner, orphan and widow
rationale: The Lord’s guarding newcomers and taking up orphan and widow corresponds to His judgment for sojourner, orphan and widow and love for the sojourner. Different descriptions of care remain distinct.

relationship: The Lord reigns for ever
rationale: The Lord’s eternal reign in Zion corresponds to the song’s declaration that He reigns for ever and ever and beyond. Psalm 145 adds the address to Zion and every generation.

relationship: Praise and music described as good or pleasing
rationale: Psalm 146 commends praise because a psalm is good and asks that praise please God; Psalm 134 commands praise because the Lord is good and music because His name is beautiful. The differing subjects of good are preserved.

relationship: Gathering Israel’s dispersed people
rationale: The Lord gathering Israel’s dispersed corresponds to His gathering Israel’s lost ones and Judah’s scattered ones from earth’s extremities. The building of Jerusalem is additional in the psalm.

relationship: Healing the brokenhearted
rationale: The Lord healing the brokenhearted closely corresponds to the commissioned speaker sent to heal the brokenhearted. Binding fractures is additional in the psalm, and the agents are not confused.

relationship: Numbering and naming the heavenly multitude
rationale: Numbering multitudes of stars and naming them corresponds to the heavenly array brought out by number and called by name. The psalm explicitly names stars; Isaiah’s upward-looking context supplies its heavenly setting.

relationship: Divine understanding beyond measure or discovery
rationale: The Lord’s understanding beyond number corresponds to the Creator’s understanding that cannot be discovered. The comparison concerns the explicit limit of human measurement or discovery, not a claim that the terms are synonymous.

relationship: The Lord raises the lowly and brings low
rationale: The Lord taking up the meek and bringing sinners to the ground corresponds to His humbling and raising high, followed by lifting the needy from earth. The psalm identifies sinners as those brought low; Samuel’s selected statement does not.

relationship: Thanksgiving with the lyre
rationale: The command to begin with thanksgiving and make music to God with a lyre closely corresponds to giving thanks to the Lord with a lyre. Psalm 32 additionally names a ten-stringed psaltery.

relationship: Rain, mountains, grass and growth for human service
rationale: Preparing rain and making grass sprout on mountains and green growth for humans corresponds to watering mountains and making grass and green plants spring up for livestock and human service.

relationship: Food for young ravens calling to the Lord
rationale: God feeding young ravens calling upon Him corresponds to the question who prepared a raven’s food, with its nestlings crying to the Lord and seeking food. Cattle are an additional group in the psalm.

relationship: Horse and human strength are not the ground of divine favor
rationale: The Lord’s lack of delight in a horse’s might or human shins corresponds to the denial that great human force or a powerful horse saves. Divine pleasure and capacity to save are related contrasts, not the same assertion.

relationship: Those fearing God and hoping in His mercy
rationale: The Lord’s pleasure in those fearing Him and hoping in His mercy corresponds to His eyes being upon those described with the same paired expressions.

relationship: Praise addressed from Zion and Jerusalem
rationale: Jerusalem and Zion are summoned to praise their God; Psalm 134 blesses the Lord from Zion and identifies His dwelling in Jerusalem. This compares the named city and its worship without dating the headings.

relationship: God feeds with the finest wheat
rationale: The Lord filling the city with the finest wheat closely corresponds to His feeding them with the finest wheat. The source’s peaceful borders and target’s honey are distinct additional provisions.

relationship: Snow and wool in paired imagery
rationale: The psalm compares snow with wool, while Isaiah compares the whitening of sins with snow and wool. The shared pair supports a limited image comparison; mist like ashes and moral cleansing remain different subjects.

relationship: Ice and frost within divine rule over water
rationale: God casting ice like morsels and the question who withstands His cold correspond to Job’s questions about the origin of ice and frost and the fixing of the abyss’s face. The target’s actual flowing-water wording is retained, without replacing it with another edition’s congealing phrase.

relationship: Divine breath or wind controls frost and water
rationale: The Lord blowing wind so waters flow, after sending His word to melt ice, corresponds to frost given from the Strong One’s breath and His steering water as He wishes. Frost-giving and melting are different actions.

relationship: Word and law declared to Jacob and Israel
rationale: God declaring His word, ordinances and judgments to Jacob and Israel corresponds to raising a testimony in Jacob and setting a law in Israel. The named people and divine instruction coincide, with distinct terms for that instruction.

relationship: Israel’s distinctive divine judgments among nations
rationale: The claim that no other nation received this disclosure of judgments corresponds to the rhetorical question whether another great nation has such righteous ordinances and judgments. The comparison preserves the distinction between assertion and question.

relationship: The heavens summoned to praise
rationale: The summons to praise from the heavens and highest places corresponds to the summons for heavens and earth to praise. The target extends the range to sea and its creeping creatures.

relationship: All angels and powers summoned to worship
rationale: The paired summons to all God’s angels and powers to praise Him corresponds to the paired commands that all His angels and powers bless Him. Psalm 102 adds their doing His word and will.

relationship: The heavenly lights called to praise their maker
rationale: Sun, moon, stars and light are summoned within the psalm’s creation praise; Genesis describes the two great lights and stars set in heaven. The psalm’s named sun and moon are not substituted into Genesis’ wording.

relationship: Waters above heaven
rationale: The praise summons naming water above the heavens corresponds to the creation account’s water above the firmament, which God names Heaven. The heavens of heavens remain the psalm’s additional expression.

relationship: Creation by divine speech and command
rationale: The reason for praise repeats the sequence that He spoke and they came to be, He commanded and they were created. This is a close verbal correspondence.

relationship: Creation endures under God’s established word
rationale: The enduring establishment and command that will not pass away correspond to God’s word remaining in heaven, the founded earth remaining, and all things serving His arrangement. The exact subjects and time expressions remain distinct.

relationship: Earth and its watery realm summoned to praise
rationale: The summons from earth to dragons and deeps corresponds to heavens, earth, sea and everything creeping in them being summoned to praise. Dragons are not identified with a particular creature in the target.

relationship: Fire and wind in divine service
rationale: Fire and storm wind fulfilling God’s word can be compared with His angels as winds and ministers as burning fire. The relation is the explicit fire-and-wind service imagery, without deciding whether the two passages identify the same beings.

relationship: Trees rejoicing or praising before the Lord
rationale: The summons to fruit trees and cedars to praise corresponds to all woodland trees exulting before the coming Lord. The psalm’s mountains and hills are not inserted into the target.

relationship: Land creatures in creation and praise
rationale: The praise list of wild animals, cattle and creeping things corresponds to those kinds named in the creation of land animals. Winged birds are additional in the source, not in the selected target.

relationship: Peoples and kingdoms assembled for the Lord’s praise
rationale: Earth’s kings, peoples, rulers and judges are summoned to praise; Psalm 101 joins the declaration of His praise to peoples and kingdoms gathering to serve Him. The target does not separately name judges.

relationship: The Lord’s name and unique exaltation
rationale: The Lord’s name alone being exalted corresponds to the declaration that His name is Lord and He alone is Most High over all the earth. The source extends His praise over earth and heaven.

relationship: A horn raised for God’s people or the righteous
rationale: Raising a horn of His people corresponds to the righteous person’s horns being raised, after sinners’ horns are broken. The image is shared without identifying a particular ruler or event.

relationship: The summons to sing a new song
rationale: Both passages command a new song to the Lord. Psalm 149 places praise in the assembly of holy ones; Psalm 95 summons all earth and includes a different heading.

relationship: Praise in the assembly of holy ones
rationale: Praise in the assembly of holy ones corresponds to acknowledgment of the Lord’s truth in an assembly of holy ones. The heavens are explicitly named in Psalm 88, without being inserted as the source assembly’s identity.

relationship: Israel’s maker and king
rationale: The summons for Israel to rejoice in its maker and Zion’s children in their king corresponds to the Lord who made and formed chosen Israel and identifies Himself as Israel’s King. The target’s Jacob address and womb imagery remain its own.

relationship: Timbrel and collective song to the Lord
rationale: Praising in a chorus with tambourine and psaltery can be compared with Miriam and the women using timbrels and dances as she leads the song to the Lord. Instruments, chorus and dancing are not treated as identical terms or one performance.

relationship: The meek lifted by the Lord
rationale: The Lord exalting the meek in salvation corresponds to His taking up the meek in Psalm 146. The source also states His pleasure in His people, and the target contrasts sinners brought low.

relationship: Rejoicing and remembrance upon the bed
rationale: The holy ones rejoicing upon their beds can be compared with remembrance of God upon the speaker’s bed and exultation in the shelter of His wings. The target does not explicitly place all of its exultation on the bed.

relationship: Two-edged swords in literal and comparative use
rationale: The holy ones hold two-edged swords while exalting God; Hebrews describes God’s word as sharper than any two-edged sword. The distinctive weapon expression is shared without making the psalm’s held swords a metaphor for the word.

relationship: Vengeance and judgment upon enemies among nations
rationale: The purpose of executing vengeance and reproof among nations can be compared with the Lord’s declared repayment to enemies and vengeance for His sons’ blood. The psalm’s holy ones and Deuteronomy’s divine agent are distinguished; no specific written judgment is identified.

relationship: Kings subjected to judgment and fetters
rationale: The poetic binding of kings in fetters can be compared with the narrated judgment and fettering of King Sedekias. The historical captors are Babylonian, not identified as the psalm’s holy ones, and this is not asserted to fulfill the psalm.

relationship: Praise in heavenly and holy assembly language
rationale: Praise among God’s holy ones and in the firmament of His power corresponds to the heavens acknowledging His wonders and an assembly of holy ones acknowledging His truth. This does not resolve the identity of every holy one.

relationship: Praise according to greatness and mighty acts
rationale: Praise for mighty acts and abundant greatness corresponds to the Lord’s limitless greatness and the generations declaring His power and fearsome acts. The connection follows the explicit grounds for praise.

relationship: Trumpets and stringed instruments in praise
rationale: The summons to praise with trumpet, psaltery and lyre can be compared with appointed praise before the ark using harps, lyres and trumpets. The psaltery is not equated with every instrument name in Chronicles, and no performance date for the psalm is inferred.

relationship: Tambourine and chorus in praise
rationale: The summons to praise with tambourine and chorus closely corresponds to praising God’s name in a chorus and making music with tambourine and psaltery. Each passage retains its different additional instruments.

relationship: Sounding cymbals in joyful praise
rationale: The command to praise with sounding cymbals corresponds to David’s appointment of singers and instruments to sound with gladness, including bronze cymbals. The source’s cymbals of a shout are not treated as a technical name found in Chronicles.

relationship: The closing summons extends praise to all living voices
rationale: Let every breath praise the Lord corresponds to the closing summons for all flesh to bless His holy name. The collective scope and closing praise function are shared, while breath and flesh remain distinct expressions.

relationship: David the youngest brother tending the flock
rationale: The psalm’s small and younger David shepherding his father’s sheep corresponds to Jesse’s remaining youngest son tending the flock before being summoned. The narrative does not repeat every adjective in the psalm.

relationship: Goliath and the single-combat setting
rationale: The full heading places David’s fight with Goliath in single combat; Samuel identifies Goliath and records his challenge for two men to fight in single combat. The psalm’s outside-the-number statement remains its own heading metadata.

relationship: David’s hands and musical instruments
rationale: David’s making an instrument and fitting a psaltery with his hands and fingers can be compared with his skill in playing and his hand playing the kinyra before Saul. Making and playing are different acts, and the instrument names are not equated.

relationship: The Lord hears without human limitation
rationale: The assertion that the Lord Himself hears corresponds to the rhetorical question whether the One who planted the ear does not hear. This explains the shared hearing claim without assigning an unstated messenger to the source question.

relationship: David taken from the sheep and anointed
rationale: The account of being taken from the father’s sheep and anointed with oil corresponds to David summoned from the flock and anointed by Samuel. Psalm 151 names His angel while Samuel names Samuel; their identity is not resolved by the supported shepherd-to-anointing sequence.

relationship: Appearance does not secure the brothers’ election
rationale: The handsome and tall brothers in whom the Lord takes no pleasure correspond to the warning not to regard Eliab’s appearance or height and the rejection of Jesse’s sons passing before Samuel. The narrative’s appearance warning is directed particularly at Eliab, not asserted of every brother.

relationship: The foreigner curses David by his gods
rationale: The source’s going out to the foreigner and being cursed by his idols corresponds to Goliath confronting David and cursing him by his gods. The different idols and gods wording is preserved.

relationship: David removes the foreigner’s head with his own sword
rationale: Both passages describe David taking the opponent’s sword and removing his head. The psalm adds the removal of Israel’s reproach; the narrative records the foreigners fleeing when their champion died.
